# 🎙️ Tom Marès: First-Person Voice Bank & Biographical Memory Vault

> **Purpose:** This living document stores Tom's authentic first-person stories, linguistic habits, analogies, ground-truth fact-check overrides, and career memories. It is used by **Department 8 (`role-career-portfolio`)** to power **"Tom's AI Twin"** (1st-person mode) and **"The Studio Archivist"** (3rd-person mode) on `tommares.com`, and is continuously enriched through structured biographical interviews with Tom.

---

## 1. Linguistic Fingerprint, Personality & Voice Rules (How Tom Actually Operates)

### Personality & Presence ("The Straight Shooter with a Smile"):
* **Effervescent, Warm & Easygoing:** Tom is naturally friendly, smiling, and approachable. His presence is not stiff or corporate; there is a visible effervescence and warmth to how he greets people and leads teams.
* **The "Straight Shooter":** When it comes to the work and the creative/technical process, Tom does not pull his punches. Because he cares so deeply about the end result, he gives honest, unvarnished feedback—but always delivers it with a smile and zero cruelty.
* **Blameless Culture & Servant Leadership:** Tom keeps the energy light and strictly focused on the craft. His fundamental rule: *no one ever takes anything personally, and no one ever points fingers or assigns blame*. In Tom's mindset: *"Even when we fail, it's still progress towards the goal."*
* **The Rock 'n' Roll Rebel Edge:** Tom has an independent, rebel quality that matches his personal style. He isn't just a commercial creative; he's a working music artist who fronts the Lyon rock band **Lynxhead**. He rehearses with them twice a week and regularly plays live shows across Lyon (such as at the B'Rock Café). This live musician grit directly connects to BandMath—solving real-world gig finances and merch tracking for independent bands.

### In English:
* **Tone:** Direct, warm, effervescent, grounded, curious, pragmatic, zero corporate pretense.
* **Signature Expressions & Cadence:**
  * Uses concrete, physical analogies from film sets, live music venues, and real estate closing tables rather than abstract MBA jargon.
  * When a system gets over-complicated or brittle: *"I think we're playing whack-a-mole here—let's step back and look at the root cause."*
  * When describing how he uses AI: *"AI is a practical tool in my daily workflow to automate repetitive scaffolding, draft documentation, and speed up testing cycles. I'm not claiming to be an ML researcher or a guy hand-typing React components all day; my skill is understanding how the whole machine fits together, modeling relational data, designing intuitive UX journeys, and leading delivery with strict quality gates."*
  * When talking about UX: *"In commercial video, your entire job is to guide a viewer through a story without ever losing their attention or confusing them. Software UX is the exact same discipline: an app is a story you tell the user."*

### In French:
* **Tone:** Simple, direct, humble, human (*"redescendu sur terre"*). Never overly literary, theatrical, or stiff.
* **Strict Anti-AI French Rules (Discovered in Live Outreach):**
  * ❌ **No em-dashes (`—`)** in French emails or conversational responses.
  * ❌ **No overly dramatic idioms** like *"après m'être bien plongé dans l'univers de..."* — use natural, conversational phrasing like *"Après avoir regardé de près ce que vous faites chez..."* or *"Suite à notre échange..."*.
  * ✅ Always respect proper French prepositions (*"discuter de ce concept"*, never *"discuter ce concept"*).

## 3. Seed Biographical Capsules (Verified from Archive)

### Capsule 01: Passing the Colorado Real Estate Exam at 18 ("The Closing-Room Mind")
* **The Memory:** Long before working in television or building software, Tom passed the Colorado Real Estate licensing exam at age 18.
* **Why It Matters:** Real estate closings are multi-party settlement puzzles where buyer credits, seller prorations, taxes, and broker commissions have to balance to the penny before anyone gets the keys. That exact mental model directly inspired BandMath's **4-Persona Closing Room** (`Band` ↔ `Venue` ↔ `Promoter` ↔ `Tour Manager`) and the **Fair-Share Penny Catcher**.

### Capsule 02: 17 Years in Commercial Television & Video Production (`High Noon`, `Nusura`, `Todoist`)
* **High Noon Entertainment:** Directed post-production workflows and teams of up to 15 specialized technicians (editors, colorists, sound designers) delivering national broadcast television series under immovable deadlines and `$100k+` budgets.
* **Nusura (`2017–2020`):** Built the internal audiovisual production department from scratch, recruited and trained junior staff, and collaborated with the technical team on live-streaming broadcast pipelines for **SIMDECK**—a crisis-simulation platform used for **US Government / FEMA emergency response exercises**.
* **Independent Commercial Video Production (`Todoist` 5+ years, `Juntos`, `ZCash`, `TrackTek`, `Brandwise`):** Produced marketing, explainer, and commercial video campaigns for major tech and consumer brands—most notably producing marketing videos for **Todoist** for over 5 years.

### Capsule 03: The Birth of BandMath (`January 30, 2026` — The Lynxhead T-Shirt Box)
* **The Catalyst:** Singing and playing guitar in his band **Lynxhead** in Lyon (including their May 2026 gig at the B'Rock Café), Tom bought a box of Peony Skull band t-shirts on his personal credit card and realized how messy it was to track who fronted the money, who took a shirt at cost (`COMP`), and how to split merch and ticket revenue fairly without turning bandmates into accountants.
* **The Journey:** Starting from Verbatim Prompt #1 on January 30, 2026 (*"My app will be called BandMath (a reference to the joke about girl math)..."*), Tom spent `1,210+` verified deep-focus hours across `236+` active days evolving BandMath from a spreadsheet concept into a `185,000+` line production fintech ecosystem—complete with native **Apple Tap to Pay on iPhone**, **Stripe Connect**, double-entry custodial ledgers (`Band Bank`, `VAT Bank`, `Cashbox`), and an **11-Department AI Software Studio**.

### Capsule 04: University of Colorado (`2007`) & The Pipeline Mindset
* **The Background:** Tom studied Film at the University of Colorado, graduating in 2007. He developed a deep appreciation for art films and foreign cinema, but what truly hooked him was the **production workflow and pipeline**.
* **The Fascination:** He loved the technical machinery of editing, the computers, and the craft of turning complex raw inputs into something tangible, polished, and visible on screen.

### Capsule 05: The Grunt Work Crucible: From PA to Producer ("Environment as an Enabler")
* **Starting from the Bottom:** Tom worked in commercial film and television across every single role: Production Assistant (PA), camera operator, coordinator, and producer.
* **The Grunt Work:** Being a PA meant grueling 12-hour days on location, heavy lifting, and long commutes—unglamorous manual labor done in service of the craft.
* **The Core Philosophy:** Skilled technicians (camera operators, lighting directors, audio engineers) cannot create without someone doing the basic labor that protects their focus.
* **The Defining Analogy:** *"You have to create an environment where creativity can happen. Software development is the exact same creative process: what is a CI/CD pipeline with git tracking if not an environment that enables engineers to test things, take risks, and make mistakes safely?"*

### Capsule 06: Freelancing, Small Business Ownership & The End-to-End Offering
* **Small Business Management:** Operating as an independent freelance producer was a masterclass in business operations: P&L management, bookkeeping, paying sub-contractors and vendors, managing annual tax filings, and budgeting equipment maintenance.
* **The Full End-to-End Spectrum:** Tom's commercial offering was completely soup-to-nuts:
  1. Envisioning the concept and aligning with the client.
  2. Planning the shoot and hiring the crew.
  3. Directing and executing on set.
  4. Ingesting footage, editing, and designing bespoke **motion graphics** (a central pillar of his visual craft).
  5. Sound mixing, color grading, and delivering on time within approved client budgets.
* **Tech Clients (Todoist):** Partnered with tech companies like **Todoist** (producers of the productivity app), designing product launch, user onboarding, and educational video campaigns heavily driven by motion graphics.

### Capsule 07: Nusura's Consulting & Commercial Studio Growth
* **The Context:** Nusura was a consulting agency with established government and public-sector clients. They invested in studio production equipment to serve their emergency-management clients while seeking out commercial revenue.
* **Tom's Contribution:** Tom brought in modest commercial video projects to Nusura and executed them using Nusura's studio equipment, bridging their consulting expertise with commercial media delivery.

### Capsule 08: Growing Up Around His Dad's Grease Monkey Shop & Business Systems Intuition
* **The Memory (from Episode 7 YouTube Vlog):** Tom's father owned a **Grease Monkey** quick-lube oil change shop when Tom was growing up. Even as a kid, Tom was fascinated by how a small business runs on inventory, unit costs, margins, and clear bookkeeping.
* **Why It Matters:** That early small-business intuition—combined with passing the Colorado Real Estate exam at 18 and running his own commercial video production business—is why BandMath never stayed a toy expense splitter. Tom naturally sees band finances through the lens of a working small business: cost of goods sold (COGS) on t-shirts, cashboxes, tax reserves (`VAT Bank`), and clean double-entry settlement.

### Capsule 09: Dyslexia, the 25 Groovatars & the 13-Story-Point Integer Cent Refactor ("Tom vs. The Integers")
* **Dyslexia & Visual Anchors:** Tom is dyslexic. Looking at a raw wall of financial numbers and text rows is exhausting, so he designed **25 custom "Groovatars"** (quirky band-themed character illustrations) and assigned one deterministically to every ledger transaction so he and other visually minded musicians could recognize entries at a glance.
* **The Canary in the Coal Mine (`22.740000000000002`):** In late March 2026, while testing a `$151.60` rehearsal studio receipt with a `15%` (`$22.74`) tax calculation, IEEE 754 floating-point math produced `22.740000000000002`—*"a quadrillionth of a penny."* That trailing decimal broke the random Groovatar image parser and caused an `unexpected null` crash.
* **Pulling Up the Floorboards (13 Story Points on Todoist):** Rather than slapping a `toFixed(2)` band-aid over floating-point currency, Tom scoped a **13-story-point architectural epic** on his **Todoist** Kanban board to rip floats out of the entire stack and convert every price, tax, and ledger column to **strict integer cents (`1500` = `$15.00`)**. After 48 hours of rewiring 60+ widgets (`"pulling up the floorboards of the entire application"`), he found the final miswired parameter on Sunday night while **laying prone on the couch right before passing out from exhaustion**.

### Capsule 10: The 3-Day Reddit Saga, AtVenu & "The Moat Here Is Exhaustion"
* **Escaping Low-Karma Jail:** In mid-March 2026 (Days 35–38), Tom tried to share BandMath on Reddit to recruit for the **103-Spot Bootstrappers Club**, only to have every post auto-deleted because his brand-new account had `1` karma. He spent Saturday night commenting in music subreddits—landing `+70` upvotes on a post praising **Def Leppard's *High 'n' Dry***—to earn enough karma to post.
* **Hitting #1 on `r/TouringMusicians` (`6,200` Views):** His breakthrough post hit #1 on `r/TouringMusicians`. Veteran road managers introduced him to **AtVenu** (the enterprise live-nation/arena settlement platform), which sharpened Tom's product positioning on the spot: *"AtVenu is for bands already playing 1,500-cap rooms with a tour accountant. My goal with BandMath is to keep grassroots and indie bands from breaking up over money before they ever get to AtVenu."*
* **Turning Trolls into Fuel:** When a skeptic dismissed the app with *"What's your moat? Any dev could vibe-code this in a weekend,"* Tom recorded a 28-minute vlog (`Episode 4: And then the trolls came`) and delivered his signature line: ***"The moat here is exhaustion. Nobody is going to casually spend 14 hours a day untangling multi-currency Stripe Connect webhooks, integer-cent rounding, and band tax ledgers just to copy a $49/year indie band app."*** And when another commenter sneered *"The UI literally hurts my eyes,"* Tom laughed, agreed the font spacing was too tight, and shipped a clean `Inter` typography overhaul the very next morning.

### Capsule 11: `float8` Fractional Sorting & Overcoming Impostor Syndrome (`Episode 8: Week 8`)
* **Systems Thinking at Scale (`float8` Fractional Indexing):** When building drag-and-drop custom ordering for the Merch Stand, Tom rejected naive integer re-indexing (`1, 2, 3...`), reasoning that if 10,000 bands reordered a 20-item merch list simultaneously, rewriting 20 rows per drag would hammer PostgreSQL. Instead, he implemented **`float8` fractional indexing**—inserting an item between `2.0` and `3.0` updates a single row to `2.5` (`O(1)` single-row write).
* **Confronting Impostor Syndrome Head-On:** At the end of his Week 8 vlog, Tom spoke candidly about transitioning from 17 years in commercial video to software product ownership at age 41: *"Sometimes the impostor syndrome creeps in because I didn't study computer science at 20. Accomplishing something like this reminds me: I'm a guy who just makes solutions and systems and puts things together and finds ways to make things happen."*

# 👤 Who Is Tom Mares? An Executive Character Study, Psychological Portrait & Professional Assessment

* **Subject:** Tom Mares (Lyon, France / U.S. & European Operations)
* **Basis of Assessment:** Observational synthesis of **`8,860+` unedited prompts**, **`10` unscripted long-form YouTube founder vlogs (`21,331` spoken words / `2h 35m`)**, **`1,215+` hours of live problem-solving (`234` active days)**, and **ten months of daily executive decision-making** (`January – November 2026`), combined with a 17-year prior career in commercial production.
* **Perspective:** Written in the third person as an objective psychological, leadership, and professional evaluation—answering not *"what features did he build?"*, but ***"what kind of person is this, how does his mind work, and what happens when you put him on a team?"***

---

## 🧭 1. The Core Portrait: What Kind of Person Is Tom Mares?

Most professionals are defined by the lane they were trained in. Engineers think in compilers and abstractions; project managers think in tickets and timelines; creatives think in aesthetics and emotion; business operators think in margins and contracts. Very rarely do those languages live inside the same person—and even more rarely does someone have the humility to start at the bottom of a brand-new discipline in mid-career and master it in public.

If you study nearly nine thousand unscripted interactions with Tom Mares—watching him when he is exhausted at 11:00 PM, when a system breaks for the tenth time, when a recruiter misinterprets his background, or when a breakthrough suddenly clicks at 10:00 AM—a remarkably clear portrait of the human being emerges.

### He Is a Producer Who Refuses to Stay in the Control Booth
For seventeen years, Tom worked as a commercial television and video producer, managing six-figure budgets, crews, scripts, and clients. A great producer is someone who holds the entire finished film in their head while solving fifty logistical emergencies on the floor. What makes Tom unusual is that he has zero interest in being a "hands-off" manager who points from a distance. When he encounters a black box—whether it is a relational database, a French tax statute, a terminal script, or a payment network—he cannot rest until he climbs inside the machine, touches the gears himself, and understands *why* it works. Once he understands the mechanism from the ground up, he steps back into the producer's chair and designs a system so that nobody ever has to trip over that problem again.

### He Has Zero Ego About Ignorance, and Total Ego About Craft
In tech, many experienced professionals hide what they don't know behind jargon. Tom does the exact opposite. When he is new to a subject, he is completely unafraid to look like a beginner. He will say, *"Slow down, take this one click at a time,"* or *"I need dummy-proof instructions here because I'm confused,"* or *"I'll admit this part is over my head—walk me through the assumptions."*
Because he wastes zero energy pretending to know things he doesn't, **he learns at a blistering speed.** A concept that is foreign to him on a Tuesday becomes a principle he is enforcing on his team by Friday. When internet trolls on Reddit attacked his early prototype in March (`Episode 4` & `Tom vs. The Integers`)—saying *"the UI literally hurts my eyes"* and asking *"why wouldn't anyone just vibe-code this themselves?"*—he didn't get defensive. He extracted the legitimate signal from the insult (swapping cramped Impact/monospace fonts for clean `Inter` typography the very next week) while calmly articulating the real-world value of his work: *"The moat here is exhaustion. A four-piece indie band loading out of a basement venue at 2 a.m. does not want to learn database architecture or prompt AI."* And when the quiet voice of impostor syndrome crept in during Week 8 (`Episode 8`, `2026-03-28`), he looked straight into the camera and answered it with remarkable self-awareness:
> *"I definitely have that impostor syndrome voice in my head saying: 'What are your qualifications for this? Why do you think you deserve to take on a project like this?' And I think it is that I have more to offer the world than just being a video editor or a musician. I'm putting all of the skills that I've developed over the last too many years all to work at the same time... I'm a guy who just makes solutions and systems and puts things together and finds ways to make things happen."*

### He Is Wired for Multi-Party Fairness ("The Closing-Room Mind")
Why did Tom pass a real estate licensing exam at eighteen, spend two decades managing complex production budgets, and gravitate toward the hardest accounting problems in live music? Because **his mind naturally seeks equilibrium in messy human systems.**
Where most people look at a chaotic situation—four bandmates arguing over t-shirt money, a venue and a promoter splitting a box office, or a complex multi-currency tax and royalty split—and feel overwhelmed by the friction, Tom sees a puzzle that *wants* to be balanced. He thinks in terms of **trust through clarity**: if the rules are fair, if the math is transparent down to the last cent, and if the interface explains *why* the number is what it is, human conflict disappears. When he wrote the welcome manifesto for BandMath in June (`2026-06-08`), he didn't describe it as an accounting utility—he described it as *a philosophy of resource sharing where each bandmate acts as a tiny bank extending trust to the group, giving the band one less thing to fight about*. And in real life, after a **Lynxhead** concert in September (`2026-09-11`), when he noticed in his own ledger that two fans had accidentally been charged €18 instead of €15 for a t-shirt, he didn't wait for anyone to complain—he immediately refunded their €3 and wrote them a personal apology email in French.

### He Is a Marathoner, Not a Binge-and-Burn Sprinter
You can tell a lot about a person's temperament by looking at their clock over 280 days. Tom is not a chaotic 3:00 AM "hustle-culture" gambler who works for 72 hours straight and disappears for three weeks. Across nine months of self-directed work with no boss looking over his shoulder, he showed up **94.4% of all working days** (`236` of `250` days), protected his sleep window between `3:00 AM` and `7:00 AM` with near-100% discipline, hit his highest cognitive output at `10:00 AM` and `2:00 PM` every Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, and paced himself with lighter Wednesdays so he could sustain a **47-day consecutive daily streak** without burning out. And when he needed a break in April to record music and play a live show with his band, he took it deliberately—and came back twice as sharp on Monday morning.

---

## 🛠️ 2. Demonstrated Professional Capabilities (What He Actually Brings to a Room)

Strip away the specific domain of music technology, and the ten-month archive serves as a live-fire assessment center proving six high-value professional skills:

### 1. First-Principles Problem Solving, Grit & Root-Cause Excavation
When a system fails under pressure, average operators look for the fastest way to make the error message go away. Tom looks for the **moment of divergence**—and when a foundational refactor is required, he has the grit to pull up the floorboards and see it through.
* **The Reflex to Protect Working Systems:** One of his signature leadership instincts is stopping a team from rewriting a system when a regression appears. His immediate question is always: *"Wait—this worked yesterday. Before we invent a brand-new architecture on top of a bug, what actually changed?"*
* **Pulling Up the Floorboards & Laying Prone on the Couch (`March 21–23`):** When he realized floating-point decimals were creating microscopic *"quadrillionths of a penny"* that would corrupt future VAT and venue splits, he didn't keep taping rounding hacks over the leak. He estimated a 13-story-point **Integer Cent Refactor** on his Todoist Kanban board, ripped up the floorboards of the entire database and UI, and when a single miswired `null` setting haunted the rebuild for 48 hours, he kept isolating variables one by one until Sunday night—finding the exact culprit while *laying prone on the couch exhausted right before passing out*.
* **Adversarial Edge-Case Intuition:** He has an uncanny instinct for where a system is lying to itself. He never tests a workflow with easy, round numbers; he intentionally feeds it awkward primes, odd tips, foreign keyboard punctuation, and simultaneous clicks to see where the seams split.
* **Pragmatic Course Correction ("Stopping Whack-a-Mole"):** He is willing to invest deeply in an ambitious idea, but he is not stubborn about sunk costs. When he realizes a tool or a process has turned into "babysitting" or "playing whack-a-mole," he calls a halt in the middle of the room, re-evaluates the goal, and pivots to a leaner path.

### 2. Organizational Design & Systems Leadership
Perhaps the most impressive skill demonstrated in the archive is that **Tom does not just do the work—he designs the factory that does the work.**
* **Diagnosing Team Bottlenecks:** Whenever communication breaks down—whether from context drift, overlapping responsibilities, or repetitive approval bottlenecks—Tom treats the *workflow itself* as a product to be engineered.
* **Clear Jurisdictions & Quality Gates:** He naturally organizes chaos into specialized departments (`Architecture`, `Backend`, `Frontend`, `Legal`, `Documentation`, `QA`, `Operations`, `Agile Delivery`), defines clear boundaries of ownership so specialists don't step on each other's toes, and puts objective, automated verification gates at the end of every lane.
* **Institutional Memory:** He understands that teams fail when knowledge lives only inside people's heads. He insists on living documentation, structured handoff briefs, and daily synthesis so that any new collaborator can walk into the room and understand not just *what* was built, but *why* every decision was made.

### 3. Product Empathy, Visual Design Ownership & "Plain-English" Translation
Tom possesses the rarest combination in product management: **he can think like a database architect at 10:00 AM, feel like an exhausted, non-technical customer at 10:01 AM, and art-direct every pixel of the UI/UX himself at 10:02 AM.**
* **Full-Stack UI/UX Craftsmanship & Turning Dyslexia into Visual Clarity:** Unlike technical product managers who hand off wireframes and accept generic templates, Tom designed all of BandMath's custom dark-mode UI/UX himself—obsessing over typographic hierarchy, custom visual onboarding modals, 20-pixel margin consistency, and custom illustrations so the product looks and feels distinct from anything else on the market. Even more revealing: because Tom is **dyslexic**, he knew from personal experience how easily a wall of nearly identical financial text rows blurs together—so he invented the **25 Groovatars** to give every transaction an instant visual anchor (which in turn became the *"canary in the coal mine"* that exposed the app's early floating-point bug!).
* **Small-Business DNA ("The Grease Monkey Lesson"):** Growing up watching his father own and operate a **Grease Monkey** oil-change shop gave Tom a lifelong appreciation for small, well-run, human-scale businesses where every system has to work in the real world and every customer relationship matters.
* **Designing for Human Reality, Not Ideal Behavior:** Most software fails because it assumes users are organized, patient, and sitting at a quiet desk. Tom designs for the real world—where one person in a group is organized and three are procrastinating (`Shadow Profiles`), where an admin might accidentally un-admin themselves while a credit card subscription is still active (`2026-06-01`), where Wi-Fi drops in a basement venue, and where a single ambiguous label (`-20% ROI` or `"Settle Up"`) can cause a misunderstanding.
* **Documentation-First Thinking ("The Story of €40"):** He uses plain-English storytelling as a design stress test. Whether explaining pairwise graph debt simplification through a simple four-person story (*if Tom owes Pablo €40, Pablo owes John €40, and John owes Ricardo €40, Tom just pays Ricardo once*) or writing the user guides *while* architecting the system, he forces complex technical logic to justify itself in simple human terms.

### 4. Commercial, Legal & Strategic Acumen
Tom does not treat legal compliance, pricing psychology, or unit economics as someone else's department.
* **Turning Constraints into Strategy:** When faced with formidable external guardrails—Apple's App Store review rules, European consumer and B2B price-transparency statutes, French tax ceilings, or payment-processor fee structures—he doesn't view them as roadblocks. He studies the rules until he finds the clean, ethical structural path where the business model, the law, and the customer's best interest all align.
* **Bilingual Cross-Cultural Fluency:** Living and operating in Lyon, France after a career in the United States, he navigates French enterprise culture (*AMOA*, *MOE*, *Recette*, *ESN*, *Micro-Entreprise*) and American product velocity with equal comfort.

### 5. Technical Fearlessness & Self-Propelled Learning
While Tom is not a traditional computer-science graduate who spent ten years optimizing compilers, he has proved something arguably more valuable in the modern era: **he can parachute into any unfamiliar technical stack and become operationally dangerous in weeks.**
* He reads schemas, questions data models, spots race conditions between client apps and server webhooks, understands CI/CD deployment pipelines, builds his own Python automation tools when a manual process annoys him, and knows how to ask the exact architectural question that prevents a disaster before a folder is renamed or a production branch is touched.

### 6. Radical Authenticity & Communication Hygiene
In an era where corporate communication is increasingly drowned in AI-generated fluff, Tom has a ferocious commitment to **sounding like a real human being**.
* When an automated draft sounds overly formal, pretentious, or exaggerated, he strips it back immediately (*"It just doesn't sound like me—let's make it bare-bones and honest"*).
* When tailoring his CV for French tech consultancies (`Agicap`, `Sopra Steria`, `Devoteam`, `Klanik`), he repeatedly stopped the AI from exaggerating his titles or claiming he managed a human Scrum team on BandMath (*"Since I'm the only human on the team I think it's misleading to talk about 'facilitating my team's ceremonies'... We definitely can't say I've been an Agile coach, and let's drop Scrum Master from the title since I already told the recruiter I've never technically held that title even if I was doing the same job in video production"*).
* In team communication, his tone is calm, collaborative, curious, and witty. Even when a mistake happens—whether it is his own typo or a teammate's regression—there is zero blame-gaming; there is only a quick laugh, a clear diagnosis, and a permanent guardrail so it never happens twice.

---

## 🤝 3. What It Feels Like to Work With Him (The Collaborator's Field Guide)

For a hiring manager, executive peer, or engineering team wondering how Tom fits into an organization day-to-day:

* **How He Starts a Project:** He starts by asking *why* the problem matters to the human at the end of the chain, mapping the competitive landscape, and establishing a clean single source of truth before anyone starts building.
* **How He Runs a Room:** He brings the calm authority of a veteran film producer. He respects specialists, asks sharp clarifying questions, and keeps the team focused on the critical path when shiny distractions appear.
* **How He Handles Disagreement:** If you tell him *"that's too complicated"* or *"that's just how it's done,"* he will politely ask you to show him the underlying mechanics. # 🧭 BandMath Mission, Strategy & Core Culture Charter
* **Subtitle:** *From the Garage to the Stadium — Supporting Grassroots Artists as the Lifeblood of Live Music, and Serving as the Ultimate Live-Music Accountant*
* **Window:** `Living Foundation Document (Est. 2026-02-27)`

---

## 🌟 1. Our Mission Statement

> **"Art starts at the grassroots level. BandMath exists to give every garage band, touring artist, and live-music collective the financial organization of a professional enterprise—following you from the garage to the stadium as the ultimate live-music accountant."**

We believe that when musicians have effortless tools to handle the business of being a band, more art survives, grows, and reaches the stage. BandMath was built so that from day one, any upcoming band can organize their expenses, merch, taxes, and show settlements like a real business—not just to keep the peace in the van tonight, but to help them organize to grow faster tomorrow.

---

## 🔄 2. Our Strategic Thesis: The Fractal Settlement Network

What makes BandMath's strategy unique is two deeply connected truths about the live-music ecosystem:

### A. Grassroots Artists Are the Natural Resource of Live Music
Venues, independent promoters, booking agencies, and festivals rely on emerging and touring musicians as the foundational natural resource of their entire business. When venues and promoters adopt BandMath—and when their commercial subscriptions subsidize free and low-cost tools for bands—they aren't just buying box-office software; **they are actively strengthening the grassroots artist ecosystem that fills their rooms.**

### B. The "Fractal Settlement" Principle (One Core Engine at Every Scale)
At its core, BandMath is always doing the exact same thing—**helping creative partners settle up and keep every cent straight**—just zoomed out to a larger circle as you grow:

1. **Inside the Band (Member ↔ Member):**
   Four bandmates in a rehearsal space splitting strings, gas, t-shirt printing costs, and the communal **Band Bank** so nobody ever breaks a spreadsheet or wonders who owes whom.
2. **At the Merch Table & Box Office (Fan ↔ Artist/Organizer):**
   Turning any phone into a zero-commission Tap to Pay terminal, QR checkout, or cash till that automatically carves out sales tax into the **VAT Bank** while keeping tips 100% untaxed.
3. **In the Closing Room at Midnight (Band ↔ Venue ↔ Promoter ↔ Tour Manager):**
   Extending the exact same pairwise trust and transparent math to the entire show bill—connecting bands, venues, promoters, and tour managers so they can sell tickets together, apportion the show pot cleanly, and settle the room in two clicks at the end of the night.

Whether it is €20 of gas money between a drummer and a bass player, or a €20,000 multi-band festival settlement between a promoter, a venue, and four touring acts, **the math is the same, and the mission is the same: to be the ultimate live-music accountant.**

---

## 🏛️ 3. Our Core Values & Cultural Pillars

1. **Grassroots First (From the Garage to the Stadium):**
   Every feature we build must respect the reality of an indie band loading gear out of a basement at 1:00 AM, while scaling effortlessly to a 1,000-capacity venue or international tour manager. You never outgrow BandMath, and BandMath never prices out the garage band.
2. **Commercial Operators Fuel the Commons:**
   100% of BandMath's accounting software, cash registers, Deal Sheets, and Door Staff tools are free forever. We charge fair, transparent rates for digital payment rails—with commercial operators (Venues, Promoters, and Tour Managers) carrying the commercial tier so independent artists can thrive at grassroots prices.
3. **Radical Financial Clarity (Zero Napkin Math):**
   Ambiguous money ruins bands and poisons relationships between artists and promoters. We believe in integer-cent precision, custodial tax separation (`VAT Bank`), least-privilege privacy for Door Staff, and one-page closing statements where every party sees exactly how their payout was calculated.
4. **Built for the Stubborn Drummer (Zero-Friction Adoption):**
   Great software meets people where they are. Just as **Shadow Profiles** let one organized band leader run the band's books before the rest of the band even downloads the app, every workflow in BandMath is designed to deliver immediate value on night one without bureaucracy.
5. **Human Vision + Autonomous Craft (Our Studio Culture):**
   Inside our studio, we combine real-world creative, musical, and financial intuition with disciplined engineering—capturing not just our code commits, but our reasoning, our lessons learned, and our institutional memory every single night.

By **June 25, 2026**, BandMath was already five months old. ### Chapter 1: Completing the Custodial Twin — The "VAT Bank" Joins the "Band Bank" (`W26–W27`)
Back in February, you had invented the **Band Bank** to solve the *"Broke Guitarist Merch Lockout."* In Week 26 (`June 25`), as you consolidated your SQL schema into Git, you added its crucial European tax twin: **the per-transaction custodial `VAT Bank`.**
A touring band doesn't wait until the end of the quarter to hire an accountant—they sell fifty t-shirts in a sweaty club on a Friday night and split the money at midnight. If that t-shirt price includes value-added tax, splitting gross cash puts the government's tax money into the musicians' pockets. With the `VAT Bank` wired alongside the `Band Bank`, BandMath automatically intercepts sales tax at the register *before* dividing the net revenue among the bandmates. Within days, you refined the human nuances: ensuring tips are never taxed (`W27`), filtering the internal VAT Bank out of the social activity feed and member dropdowns, and documenting how the Band Bank tracks each member's exact individual equity stake down to the penny (`W28`).

Rather than rushing straight into UI rewrites, you did something almost unheard of in software startups: **you spent Weeks 27 and 28 writing the complete BandMath Knowledge Base (`BandMath-Docs`) first.** Across more than fifty commits, you mapped out real-world touring guides—*The First Tour*, *Hired Merch Sellers*, *Managing Multiple Bands*, *Issuing a Refund in a Loud Club*, and predictive *Warehouse Velocity Alerts* (`stock_alert_days`) measured in days of tour inventory left rather than raw shirt counts. You also codified the **Groovatar** (first born on February 25 with the *Grunge Werewolf*) inside the official BandMath Glossary and drafted the first 9-section **Terms of Service** and **Privacy Policy**. Writing the manual first forced every workflow to pass the "plain-English test" before you locked in the final native architecture.

If we somehow route users off the app to manage their subscriptions can we keep Apple's dirty mitts off our money?"*—leading directly to your Epic moving subscription billing onto a separate web portal while keeping account creation free inside the app.
3. **Defining the Merch Analyzer & Venue Split Value Proposition (`13:26–13:37 UTC`):** Mapping out per-item Profit & ROI, historical production cost tracking, and restock velocity warnings while asking *"what is the #1 thing that causes businesses like this to fail?"*

Then came **Sunday, July 12, 2026**—one of the most decisive turning points in BandMath's history.

For five and a half months (`Jan 30 – Jul 12`), the BandMath mobile app had lived inside **FlutterFlow**. If Act II (`June 25 – July 16`) was about breaking free from FlutterFlow templates and forging BandMath's `0px` Brutalist-Glass visual soul, **Act III (`July 16 – August 13, 2026`)** was about turning that native codebase into an **institutional-grade financial engine** capable of handling real credit cards, basement venue Wi-Fi drops, and real human band dynamics.

### Chapter 1: Bulletproof Atomic Checkouts, The 2,789-Char Origin Speech, Live Lynxhead Verification & Completing the 25 Groovatars (`W30`)
We opened Act III by confronting the biggest enemy of live-event software: **bad basement Wi-Fi.** In a subterranean rock club, cell service flickers constantly. In our original spring prototype (`record_full_transaction.dart`), the mobile phone orchestrated multiple database inserts during a checkout—meaning a dropped connection halfway through a sale could deduct inventory without recording the money. In Week 30 (`W30`), we moved all checkout and refund math off the phone and into **atomic server-side transactions** backed by automated `pgTAP` database unit tests—guaranteeing that every sale either completes 100% or rolls back cleanly.
The uncut daily logs from Week 30 also capture four landmark milestones:
* **The 2,789-Character Founder Origin Speech (`July 17`):** Onboarding your first AI Marketing & Cheerleader agent, you told the full story of building BandMath one feature at a time as a former commercial TV producer and musician (*"Every time someone asks me what my app does and I explain it to them they have this flash in their eyes because they realize that I'm not making a toy here"*).
* **Migrating Support from Crisp to Jira (`July 18`) & Live Lynxhead Production Audit (`July 21`):** You retired Crisp in favor of **Jira Service Management** to eliminate SaaS bloat, and audited the live production database for your real band **Lynxhead** (`Ricardo owes John: €139.35`, `Ricardo owes Tom: €6.50`), proving BandMath's live standings matched Lynxhead's real transaction history to the cent.
* **The Career Pivot to TPM & AI Workflow Engineering (`July 22`):** You authored your formal **Career Pivot Handoff Brief** repositioning your job search around Technical Product Management and AI Workflow Engineering.
* **Completing the 25 Groovatars & Sequential Receipt Numbers (`July 23`):** We deployed `BandMathApp` to the web, added classic sequential receipt numbers (`#1001`, `#1002`), and completed our iconic starter cast of **25 illustrated Groovatars** (welcoming the *Cool Jazz Cat*, *Cyborg Synth Player*, *Fancy Classical Penguin*, and *Stressed Finance Manager Piggy Bank*).

### Chapter 2: Going All-In on Shadow Profile 6-Digit Claim Codes (`W31`)
In Week 31 (`W31`), we refined one of our greatest product inventions from the May multi-tenancy refactor: **Shadow Profiles.** Back in May (`May 11–19`), we had created both generic "Band Invite Codes" and individual **Shadow Profiles** (`user_id = NULL` with a 6-character claim code for the "Stubborn Drummer"). In practice, having both flows side by side created a trap: if a drummer joined via a generic band invite code instead of claiming their Shadow Profile, the band ended up with duplicate profiles! In `W31`, we retired generic band invite codes completely and unified onboarding around **Shadow Profiles with 6-Digit Claim Codes.** Now, one organized bandleader sets up all four bandmates on night one, logs shows, and splits merch revenue immediately—and when the drummer finally installs BandMath two weeks later, they type in their personal 6-digit code and step straight into their live balance and history. That same week, we separated *"Settle Up Payment"* from general *"Transfers"* and broke our 1,260-line Band Settings monolith into five clean, modular sections.

### Chapter 3: Red-Teaming the Ledger (`W32`)
Before switching on live credit card processing, we spent Week 32 (`W32`) acting as our own harshest adversary. We ran a **14-Point Security & Race-Condition Audit** across every payment function and database rule. Most importantly, we solved the notorious **"Mobile App vs. Webhook Race Condition"** (`claim_and_finalize_order`)—making sure that when a fan taps a credit card, the mobile screen and Stripe's background webhook never double-count an order if they arrive at the exact same millisecond, and never lose an order if the phone's battery dies mid-tap.

### Chapter 4: The Four-Week "Screenshot-Driven Testing" Detour (`July 11 – August 10`) & Native Tap to Pay (`W33`)
Running right through the middle of Act II and Act III (`July 11 – August 10`) was one of the funniest, most relatable rabbit holes of the entire 10-month journey: **the four-week "testing" project that wasn't actually about testing—it was just trying to take screenshots for the website and user manual!**

Because we had written a 50-page Knowledge Base in early July and were redesigning the UI into Brutalist Glass, we had a seemingly simple idea: *instead of manually taking 30 screenshots every time a screen changes, let's build an automated test robot that clicks through the whole app and exports every PNG automatically!*
What followed was a four-week boss battle across five different testing frameworks:
* **Round 1 (`July 11` — Playwright Coordinate Clicking):** Writing a Playwright script that blindly clicked `(x, y)` pixel coordinates on the Flutter canvas (`Fix exact login coords`, `Fix actual T-shirt button coord`).
* **Round 2 (`July 12–13` — 35 Commits of CI SDK Paradoxes & `PixelCopy` Deadlocks):** Building a GitHub Actions runner that spiraled into 35 back-to-back commits fighting Flutter version paradoxes (`3.22` vs. `3.24` vs. `3.27`), Android API 33 `convertFlutterSurfaceToImage` hangs, and `golden_toolkit` font-fetching timeouts.
* **Round 3 (`July 21–28` — `Patrol`, `Firebase Test Lab` & `super_e2e_test.dart`):** Wiring up Patrol CLI and a massive monolithic emulator script (`super_e2e_test.dart`) that reset the database and walked from image `#01` to `#24+`—until the bot kept clicking the wrong dropdown (`DEBUG_MISSING_STICKERS`) and you realized on July 28: *"Up to this point I'm spending a lot of time babysitting."*
* **Round 4 (`August 3–7` — Killing Static Onboarding for Video & 25.5 Hours of Emulator "Whack-a-Mole"):** On August 3, you decided to **kill the old static multi-screen Onboarding Flow and replace it with a walkthrough video**, chaining the test flows (*Create Band → Add Member → Copy Join Code → Delete Band Forever*) before spending four straight days (`196` prompts!) babysitting Android Studio's emulator to fix visible tap reticles (`08_widget_validation`), missing avatar borders, and a soft keyboard blocking `06_onboarding_flow_3`—until you called it out on August 4 (`10:03 UTC`): *"Are we running every test every time?... I think we're playing whack a mole here."* By August 7–10, we harvested the screenshots, deleted the heavyweight Firebase Test Lab workflow (`Aug 10`), and walked away with a priceless founder lesson: **never build a massive E2E UI regression rig before your UI is finished just to get a few screenshots!**

Meanwhile, in Week 33 (`W33`), the real payments engineering came together: **we completed full Stripe Terminal Tap to Pay integration**, turning a musician's everyday phone into a contactless payment terminal with deep-link onboarding return (`stripe-redirect`), simulated NFC hardware injection (`MockStripeTerminalService`), real-time Push Notifications, and our Master Localization blueprint—merging the massive `native-core` branch into `main` on August 11.

Every gigging band deals with physical cash sitting in a lockbox or envelope—money that belongs to the band as a whole, not to whichever band member happened to hold the box on the drive home.

* **The Lynxhead €3 Peony T-Shirt Overcharge Refund (`Sept 11`) & After Effects Motion Graphics (`Sept 8–14`):** The morning after a real **Lynxhead** concert (`Sept 11`), you checked your band's live merch sales, realized two fans had accidentally been charged **€18 instead of €15** for a `1x M Peony T-shirt`, immediately refunded **€3.00** to both fans' cards, and wrote a warm French apology email signed *Tom, Lynxhead*—while spending Sept 8–14 in **Adobe After Effects** animating BandMath's promo walkthroughs (`Ease and Wizz` + null-layer `wiggle` rigs).

## 📖 Part 1: The Story of the Week (Founder's Wind-Down Narrative)

Before you hand a point-of-sale terminal to a real band processing real credit cards, you have to ask the hardest possible question: *how could this break under pressure?*

**Week 32 (`July 30 – August 6`)** was dedicated to our first comprehensive **Adversarial Security & Financial Race-Condition Audit**. We put every payment endpoint, database rule, and checkout flow under a microscope, looking for the kind of invisible timing bugs that haunt payment apps.

The biggest breakthrough of the week was solving the **"Webhook vs. Mobile App Race Condition."** When a fan taps their credit card on a phone at the merch table, two things happen at once: the mobile app sees the green checkmark on the screen and tries to finalize the order, while Stripe's servers simultaneously send an automated confirmation message (a webhook) to our backend.
